title: Benchmarking Granularity
summary: Design a multi-granularity benchmarking strategy that combines end-to-end, macro, and micro evaluations to diagnose system bottlenecks.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Design a multi-granularity benchmarking strategy that combines end-to-end, macro, and micro evaluations to diagnose system bottlenecks
- Classify benchmark scenarios into micro, macro, and end-to-end granularity levels based on workload scope
- Compare the diagnostic power and real-world representativeness across micro, macro, and end-to-end benchmarks
- Evaluate why a microbenchmark speedup does not by itself determine end-to-end service speedup
- Apply roofline model principles to estimate the throughput ceiling at low arithmetic intensity relative to peak compute capability

A kernel that runs … faster in isolation may deliver no end-to-end speedup if the data pipeline cannot keep the accelerator fed. In an illustrative request, a … inference speedup applied to a … model stage inside a … request yields only about a … end-to-end improvement, or less if the optimization increases memory pressure. The dilution makes the measurement boundary a design choice. Carpentry specifies *how* a measurement is built, while **benchmarking granularity** specifies *what* physical boundary it measures.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Micro benchmarks
- Macro benchmarks
- End-to-end benchmarks
- End-to-end vs. component latency
- Granularity trade-offs and selection criteria

Pay attention to: Granularity spectrum: micro, macro, end-to-end, system-in-the-loop; Diagnostic power vs. real-world representativeness trade-off; Profiler tools (framework vs kernel profilers); Amdahl's law and component isolation pitfalls.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Compare microbenchmarks, macrobenchmarks, and end-to-end benchmarks along the axes of diagnostic isolation and real-world representativeness.
blocks.md:
Benchmarking granularity exists on a fundamental trade-off curve between diagnostic isolation and real-world representativeness:
- Microbenchmarks (e.g., isolated GEMM kernels) offer high diagnostic isolation—pinpointing exact hardware execution bottlenecks or compiler code generation efficiency—but low real-world representativeness because they ignore framework overhead, memory transfers, and surrounding pipeline stages.
- Macrobenchmarks (e.g., full ResNet or Transformer forward passes) offer moderate diagnostic power and moderate representativeness, evaluating model architecture and framework execution while excluding external I/O.
- End-to-end benchmarks (e.g., full serving pipelines with network ingestion, preprocessing, inference, and database writes) offer high real-world representativeness—capturing true user experience—but low diagnostic isolation because a latency spike could stem from network congestion, garbage collection, data loading, or compute.

questions.q: An e-commerce search service reports that production query latency has increased by \$40\%, violating its SLA. Which benchmarking workflow represents the most effective top-down diagnostic strategy?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. A disciplined top-down diagnostic workflow starts at the end-to-end level to isolate which pipeline stage caused the SLA violation, zooms into macrobenchmarks (subgraphs/models) for that component, and finally uses microbenchmarks and kernel profilers (e.g. Nsight) to identify the specific hardware or algorithmic bottleneck. Rewriting kernels blindly wastes effort on non-bottlenecks; testing memory bus bandwidth in isolation does not pinpoint where time is spent in the request path; testing tokenization alone ignores interactions with database retrieval and model execution.
questions.hint: Think about: design a multi-granularity benchmarking strategy that combines end-to-end, macro, and micro evaluations to diagnose system bottlenecks.
options: Immediately rewrite all GEMM kernels in CUDA assembly without measuring the higher layers
Run isolated microbenchmarks on the GPU memory bus to determine peak DRAM bandwidth

Start with an end-to-end pipeline benchmark to isolate latency contributions across database lookup, tokenization, model inference, and reranking; next run macrobenchmarks on the slowest stage; then use microbenchmarks and kernel profilers to optimize the specific bottleneck operator
Benchmark only the isolated tokenization library on CPU and assume the rest of the pipeline is unaffected

questions.q:
Consider the following three benchmarking tasks:
(I) Timing a single \$4096 × 4096 FP16 matrix multiplication in cuBLAS.
(II) Measuring the forward-pass execution time of a complete ResNet-50 model on a single GPU.
(III) Measuring total latency for an image upload, server decompression, feature extraction, neural network classification, and database metadata write.
How are tasks (I), (II), and (III) classified by benchmarking granularity?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. Task (I) isolates an individual mathematical operator (microbenchmark); Task (II) evaluates a complete neural network architecture (macrobenchmark); Task (III) exercises the complete production data pipeline including networking, I/O, preprocessing, model execution, and storage (end-to-end system benchmark). The other combinations scramble these standardized granularity levels.
questions.hint: Think about: classify benchmark scenarios into micro, macro, and end-to-end granularity levels based on workload scope.

questions.q: If an optimized FlashAttention kernel achieves a \$4\times$ microbenchmark speedup over a standard attention implementation, the complete language model inference service hosting that model is mathematically guaranteed to run \$4\times$ faster end-to-end.
questions.explanation: False. A kernel-level speedup does not guarantee the same service-level speedup. Under fixed serial fractions and no queueing feedback, Amdahl's Law limits end-to-end improvement by the fraction of time spent in that kernel. In a loaded service, queueing and batching can also change, so the actual effect may differ from the simple fixed-fraction estimate in either direction.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate why a microbenchmark speedup does not by itself determine end-to-end service speedup.

questions.q: In roofline analysis, an accelerator has a peak compute performance of \$989\text{ TFLOP/s}$ (dense FP16) and a memory bandwidth of \$3.35\text{ TB/s}$, yielding a machine ridge point of $\RooflineRidgePoint \approx 295\text{ FLOP/byte}$. When serving a Transformer model with batch size $b=1$, the arithmetic intensity is only $I = 4.8\text{ FLOP/byte}$. What is the roofline upper bound on achieved throughput as a fraction of peak compute throughput for this workload?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Because ArithmeticIntensity < RooflineRidgePoint, the workload is memory-bandwidth bound in the roofline model. The throughput upper bound is \$3.35 TB/s × 4.8 FLOP/byte approx 16.1 TFLOP/s, and \$16.1 / 989 approx 1.6\%. This is a roofline bound on throughput relative to the matching arithmetic peak, not an observed MFU or a generic busy-utilization reading. The compute-bound answers ignore that the arithmetic intensity sits far below the ridge point.
questions.hint: Think about: apply roofline model principles to estimate the throughput ceiling at low arithmetic intensity relative to peak compute capability.
options: Approximately \$1.6\% of peak compute throughput (memory-bandwidth bound)
Exactly \$100\% because modern tensor cores execute batch b=1 at peak speed
Approximately \$50\% due to pipeline bubbles and kernel launches
Approximately \$85\% because matrix-vector multiplications are compute-bound

questions.q: An image classification inference pipeline takes \$18 ms per request in a serial CPU baseline: \$8 ms in image decoding/preprocessing and \$10 ms in neural network execution. If only the model execution is migrated to a specialized NPU that accelerates the neural network by \$5× (reducing inference time from \$10 ms to \$2 ms), with the other \$8 ms unchanged and no added transfer or queueing effects, what is the resulting end-to-end pipeline latency and speedup?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. The unchanged preprocessing still costs \$8 ms, and the accelerated model execution becomes \$10 ms/5 = 2 ms. The new serial end-to-end latency is therefore \$8+2=10 ms, and the system-level speedup is \$18/10=1.8×. The \$5× gain applies only to the model stage, not to the whole pipeline.
questions.hint: Think about: calculate end-to-end speedup in a serial pipeline when only the model-execution stage is accelerated and other latency remains fixed.

points: You can now design a multi-granularity benchmarking strategy that combines end-to-end, macro, and micro evaluations to diagnose system bottlenecks.
You can now classify benchmark scenarios into micro, macro, and end-to-end granularity levels based on workload scope.
You can now compare the diagnostic power and real-world representativeness across micro, macro, and end-to-end benchmarks.
You can now evaluate why a microbenchmark speedup does not by itself determine end-to-end service speedup.
